notes: Case studies used in GCSE and A-level geography (AQA, Edexcel, OCR, Eduqas, WJEC, SQA, CCEA), with key facts. Figures are rounded and some (especially death tolls) vary between sources: check your exam board's textbook for the figures it expects.

items.name: Nepal (Gorkha) earthquake
facts: Magnitude 7.8, at a destructive (collision) margin where the Indian Plate pushes into the Eurasian Plate
Nearly 9,000 people killed
Hundreds of thousands of homes destroyed; avalanches on Everest; landslides cut off mountain villages
Low-income country: slow rescue, dependent on international aid
items.text: The classic low-income-country earthquake case study. Compare it with a high-income example such as Christchurch or Tōhoku (Japan).

items.name: Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami, Japan
facts: Magnitude 9.0–9.1, at a destructive (subduction) margin off Japan's east coast
Tsunami waves up to about 40 m high
About 18,000 people killed or missing, most by the tsunami
Meltdowns at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant; over 150,000 people evacuated
items.text: A high-income country with the world's best earthquake preparation, still overwhelmed by the tsunami: a key example of how wealth reduces, but cannot remove, risk.

items.name: Haiti earthquake
facts: Magnitude 7.0, shallow, close to the capital Port-au-Prince
Estimates of deaths range from about 100,000 to over 300,000
About 1.5 million people made homeless
Poorly built housing, weak government and poverty made the impact far worse
items.text: Often compared with the stronger Chile earthquake of the same year, which killed far fewer people: the difference was mainly wealth and preparation.

items.name: Christchurch earthquake, New Zealand
facts: Magnitude 6.2, very shallow and close to the city centre
185 people killed
Liquefaction damaged large parts of the eastern suburbs
Much of the city centre had to be demolished and rebuilt
items.text: A high-income-country example: strong building codes and emergency services, but very high economic costs.

items.name: Indian Ocean (Boxing Day) tsunami
facts: Caused by a magnitude 9.1 earthquake off Sumatra, Indonesia
About 230,000 people killed in 14 countries, worst in Aceh (Indonesia), Sri Lanka, India and Thailand
There was no tsunami warning system in the Indian Ocean; one was set up afterwards
items.text: The deadliest tsunami recorded, and the reason the Indian Ocean now has a warning system.

items.name: Sulawesi earthquake and tsunami, Indonesia
facts: Magnitude 7.5 near the city of Palu
A tsunami and widespread liquefaction, where whole neighbourhoods slid away
More than 4,000 people killed
items.text: A recent example showing liquefaction and a tsunami in a narrow bay, where warnings failed to reach people in time.

items.name: Turkey–Syria earthquakes
facts: Magnitude 7.8 and 7.5 earthquakes on the same day, on the East Anatolian Fault
More than 55,000 people killed in Turkey and Syria
Many buildings collapsed despite building codes, raising questions about how well they were enforced
In Syria, war made rescue and aid much harder
items.text: One of the deadliest earthquakes of the century, and a powerful example of how governance affects disaster risk.

items.name: Eyjafjallajökull eruption, Iceland
facts: An eruption under an ice cap on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a constructive margin
Its ash cloud closed most of Europe's airspace for about a week
About 100,000 flights cancelled
No one was killed: local farms and roads were affected by flooding and ash
items.text: A small eruption with a huge global impact, through air travel and trade: useful for 'global interconnections'.

items.name: Typhoon Haiyan, Philippines
facts: One of the strongest tropical storms ever to reach land, with winds of about 300 km/h
A storm surge of about 5 m flooded the city of Tacloban
About 6,300 people killed
About 4 million people forced from their homes
items.text: The standard tropical storm case study for a lower-income country.

items.name: Hurricane Katrina, United States
facts: Flood defences (levees) failed and about 80% of New Orleans flooded
About 1,800 people killed
One of the costliest disasters in US history, about $125 billion
Poorer, mostly Black neighbourhoods were hit hardest and recovered slowest
items.text: A high-income-country example that shows inequality inside a rich country.
links: The United States on the map

items.name: Cyclone Idai, Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Malawi
facts: Hit the port city of Beira, Mozambique, then caused huge floods inland
More than 1,300 people killed
About 3 million people affected; cholera broke out afterwards
items.text: A recent African tropical storm case study, linked to the debate on climate change and warmer seas.

items.name: Pakistan floods
facts: Extreme monsoon rain and melting glaciers flooded about a third of the country at the peak
About 1,700 people killed and 33 million people affected
Damage and losses of about $30 billion
items.text: A case study often used for climate change and its unequal effects: Pakistan produces under 1% of the world's carbon emissions.

items.name: Australia's 'Black Summer' bushfires
facts: About 19 million hectares burned, mainly in New South Wales and Victoria
33 people killed directly by the fires; smoke affected the health of millions
About 3 billion animals killed or displaced
Followed Australia's hottest and driest year on record
items.text: Used for extreme weather, climate change and wildfire risk in a high-income country.

items.name: Somerset Levels floods, England
facts: The wettest January in southern England in records going back to 1766
Large areas of low-lying farmland were under water for weeks
About 600 homes flooded; villages such as Muchelney were cut off
Afterwards, rivers were dredged and a 20-year flood action plan was made
items.text: The key UK flood case study, often used for the debate on dredging and managing rivers.
links: The United Kingdom on the map

items.name: Boscastle flash flood, Cornwall
facts: About 75 mm of rain fell in two hours on a small, steep drainage basin
A wall of water swept through the village, carrying cars into the sea
About 100 people rescued by helicopter; no one was killed
A new flood defence scheme widened and deepened the river channel
items.text: A small, steep river basin with fast run-off: a classic UK example of a flash flood.
links: The United Kingdom on the map

items.name: Holderness coast, Yorkshire
facts: One of the fastest-eroding coastlines in Europe: about 2 m a year on average
Soft boulder clay cliffs are easily eroded by powerful North Sea waves
Towns such as Mappleton and Hornsea are protected by sea walls and rock groynes
Protecting one place can increase erosion further along the coast
items.text: The standard UK coastal erosion and management case study.
links: The United Kingdom on the map

items.name: London
facts: About 9 million people, the UK's largest city by far
A world city: a global centre of finance, culture and transport
Regeneration: the 2012 Olympic Park at Stratford, Canary Wharf and the Docklands
Challenges: housing costs, inequality and air quality
items.text: A UK major city case study (AQA and others also use Bristol, Liverpool, Birmingham, Manchester or Glasgow).
links: The United Kingdom on the map

items.name: Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
facts: About 13 million people in the metropolitan area
Around a fifth of the city's people live in favelas (informal settlements)
Favela Bairro and other schemes upgraded housing, roads and services
Hosted the 2014 World Cup final and the 2016 Olympics
items.text: The most widely used case study of a growing city in a newly emerging economy.

items.name: Lagos, Nigeria
facts: One of the largest and fastest-growing cities in Africa
Many people live in informal settlements such as Makoko, partly built on stilts over the lagoon
Big projects such as Eko Atlantic, a new city built on land reclaimed from the sea
Challenges: traffic, flooding, waste and inequality
items.text: Often used alongside the Nigeria newly-emerging-economy case study.

items.name: Mumbai, India
facts: About 20 million people in the metropolitan area; India's financial centre
Dharavi: one of Asia's largest informal settlements, home to perhaps a million people, with thousands of small businesses
Schemes to redevelop Dharavi are controversial
items.text: A city in a newly emerging economy with extremes of wealth and poverty side by side.

items.name: The Amazon rainforest
facts: The world's largest tropical rainforest, about 60% of it in Brazil
Roughly a fifth of it has been cleared since 1970, for cattle ranching, soya, logging, mining and roads
Deforestation fell sharply after 2004, rose again, and is now falling again
Home to hundreds of indigenous groups and about 10% of the world's known species
items.text: The standard tropical rainforest case study (AQA also offers Malaysia).

items.name: Malaysia's rainforests
facts: Large areas of Borneo (Sabah and Sarawak) have been cleared for palm oil plantations and logging
Malaysia and Indonesia produce most of the world's palm oil
Home to orangutans, now endangered
items.text: The alternative AQA tropical rainforest case study.

items.name: The Thar Desert, India and Pakistan
facts: One of the most densely populated deserts in the world
Opportunities: farming with irrigation (the Indira Gandhi Canal), mining, energy and tourism
Challenges: extreme heat, little water, and poor access
items.text: The hot desert case study for the 'challenges and opportunities' question (AQA also offers the Sahara).

items.name: Alaska
facts: A cold environment with permafrost, tundra and boreal forest
Opportunities: oil (the Trans-Alaska Pipeline), fishing, mining and tourism
Challenges: extreme cold, building on permafrost and inaccessibility
Climate change is warming the Arctic about four times faster than the world average
items.text: The cold environment case study (AQA also offers Svalbard).
links: The United States on the map

items.name: Nigeria: a newly emerging economy
facts: Africa's most populous country and one of its largest economies
Oil from the Niger Delta is the biggest export; oil spills have damaged the delta
Growing services, film (Nollywood), telecoms and manufacturing
Large gaps in wealth between the south and north
items.text: The AQA case study of a newly emerging economy. Explore its development with the filters.

items.name: The Aral Sea, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan
facts: Once the world's fourth-largest lake
Rivers feeding it were diverted to irrigate cotton from the 1960s
It has lost about 90% of its water; fishing ports are now in the desert
A dam (2005) has helped the northern part recover
items.text: One of the world's worst environmental disasters caused by water management: used for water security.

items.name: Three Gorges Dam, China
facts: The world's largest power station by capacity, 22.5 GW
Controls flooding on the Yangtze and lets large ships reach Chongqing
About 1.3 million people were moved from their homes
Concerns about landslides, silt and river ecosystems
items.text: A large-scale water and energy project, with clear costs and benefits.
